items.name: Ohm's law and power
items.doc: Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance (U = R × I); the electrical power is P = U × I. Any two of the four values determine the other two.
items.source: Ohm's law and Joule's law (P = U·I); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Voltage divider
items.doc: Two resistors in series divide the input voltage: V_out = V_in × R2 / (R1 + R2). The output is unloaded; for a divider that drives a load use the loaded voltage divider. The current and power are those of the divider chain itself.
items.source: Voltage divider rule; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.

items.name: Loaded voltage divider
items.doc: A voltage divider that drives a load R_L. The load is in parallel with R2, so V_out = V_in × R_P / (R1 + R_P) with R_P = R2 ∥ R_L. The unloaded output V_nl shows how much the load pulls the voltage down.
items.source: Voltage divider with a load (R2 in parallel with R_L); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a passive divider can only attenuate.
R_P must be smaller than R2; these values do not fit together (a load always pulls the lower resistance down).

items.name: Current divider
items.doc: Two resistors in parallel share the total current in inverse proportion to their resistance: I_1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2) and I_2 = I × R1 / (R1 + R2). The voltage across both is U = I_1 × R1. The two branch currents alone cannot fix the resistors, only their ratio.
items.source: Current divider rule (Kirchhoff's current law with Ohm's law); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2

items.name: Series and parallel resistors
items.doc: Resistors in series add up: R_S = R_1 + R_2 + …. Resistors in parallel combine as 1/R_P = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + …. Enter the values as a list, for example 4k7, 10k, 2k2.
items.source: Series and parallel resistor combination; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Decibel ratio
items.doc: The decibel expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale: G = 20 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for voltages and currents (field quantities) and G = 10 × log10(A_2 / A_1) for power. Choose the quantity first: +20 dB is a factor of 10 for voltages but a factor of 100 for power.
items.source: Definition of the decibel (field quantities 20·log10, power quantities 10·log10), cf. IEC 60027-3 (logarithmic quantities and their units)

items.name: dB levels
items.doc: Absolute levels in decibels: dBm is relative to 1 mW, dBV to 1 V and dBu to 0.7746 V, the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω. From a voltage and a load resistance the power follows; the derived values are shown as dBm, dBV and dBu.
items.source: Definitions: dBm = 10·log10(P / 1 mW), dBV = 20·log10(U / 1 V), dBu = 20·log10(U / 0.7746 V) with 0.7746 V = sqrt(0.6) V (1 mW in 600 Ω); decibel per IEC 60027-3

items.name: Wheatstone bridge
items.doc: A Wheatstone bridge is two voltage dividers side by side: R1 over R2 on the left and R3 over R4 on the right. The bridge voltage V_D between the two midpoints is V_D = V_S × (R2 / (R1 + R2) − R4 / (R3 + R4)). It is zero when R1 × R4 = R2 × R3; R_4b shows the R4 that balances the bridge.
items.source: Wheatstone bridge as two voltage dividers with the balance condition R1·R4 = R2·R3; e.g. C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits (resistance measurement with the Wheatstone bridge)

items.name: Star-delta transform
items.doc: Converts between a star (Y) network of three resistors R_A, R_B, R_C and the equivalent delta (Δ) network R_AB, R_BC, R_CA. Delta to star: R_A = R_AB × R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA), and cyclically. Star to delta: R_AB = (R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A) / R_C, and cyclically. Enter either the three delta or the three star resistors.
items.source: Wye-delta (star-delta) transformation; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 2
formula: rab = (ra * rb + rb * rc + rc * ra) / rc

items.name: RMS, peak and average
items.doc: Converts between the RMS value, the peak value, the peak-to-peak value and the average of the rectified waveform for a sine, square or triangle wave. The crest factor is V_pk / V_rms and the form factor is V_rms / V_avg; for a sine wave they are √2 and π / (2√2) ≈ 1.1107. The average is the mean of the absolute value (the rectified average), not the mean of the signal, which is zero for a symmetric wave.
items.source: Standard waveform relations: sine rms = peak/√2 and rectified average = 2·peak/π; square rms = rectified average = peak; triangle rms = peak/√3 and rectified average = peak/2 (integration of the waveform); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (signals)

items.name: Charge and energy
items.doc: Charge Q in ampere-hours (1 Ah = 3600 C) and energy E in watt-hours (1 Wh = 3600 J) are related by the voltage: E = Q × U. A 2 Ah cell at 3.7 V holds 7.4 Wh. The nominal voltage is only an average; real batteries deliver less energy at high load.
items.source: Definitions of charge and energy: E = Q·U (1 C·V = 1 J), 1 Ah = 3600 C, 1 Wh = 3600 J; The International System of Units (SI Brochure, BIPM)

items.name: Standard-value combiner
items.doc: Finds resistor values from a standard E series (IEC 60063) that reach a target: the nearest single value, and pairs in series or in parallel whose combined value comes closest. Enter the target resistance and choose the series in the settings (E6 to E192); every combination shows its value and its deviation from the target. In series R = R_1 + R_2, in parallel R = R_1 × R_2 / (R_1 + R_2). Example: 5 kΩ from E12 gives 4.7 kΩ + 270 Ω (−0.6 %) or 10 kΩ parallel to 10 kΩ (exactly 5 kΩ).
items.source: IEC 60063 (preferred number series E3 to E192); series and parallel resistor combination: P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: RC low-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC low-pass passes low frequencies and attenuates high ones. Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = 1 / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output phase is φ = −arctan(f / f_c) (the output lags). Above f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 10 nF give f_c ≈ 1.59 kHz; at 1 kHz the output is 84.7 % of the input (−1.45 dB) and lags by 32.1°. The formulas assume an unloaded output (load resistance much larger than R) and an ideal source.
items.source: First-order RC low-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = 1/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = −arctan(f/f_c); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: RC high-pass filter
items.doc: A first-order RC high-pass blocks low frequencies and passes high ones (a coupling capacitor with the input resistance behind it). Cutoff frequency (−3 dB point): f_c = 1 / (2π × R × C). At the test frequency f the amplitude ratio is A_v = (f / f_c) / √(1 + (f / f_c)²), the gain is G = 20 × log10(A_v) and the output leads the input by φ = arctan(f_c / f). Below f_c the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. Example with the defaults: 10 kΩ and 100 nF give f_c ≈ 159 Hz; at 100 Hz the output is 53.2 % of the input (−5.48 dB) and leads by 57.9°. The formulas assume an ideal source and an unloaded output.
items.source: First-order RC high-pass: f_c = 1/(2πRC), |H| = (f/f_c)/√(1+(f/f_c)²), φ = arctan(f_c/f); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC filters)

items.name: LC resonance
items.doc: An ideal LC circuit resonates at the Thomson frequency f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)); there the reactances are equal, X_L = X_C = √(L / C) = Z_0, the characteristic impedance. Enter any two of L, C and f_0. Example with the defaults: 100 µH and 1 nF resonate at about 503 kHz (medium-wave band) with Z_0 ≈ 316 Ω. Real coils and capacitors have losses; the RLC calculator gives the quality factor and the bandwidth.
items.source: Thomson's resonance formula f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) and Z_0 = √(L/C); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (resonant circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (frequency response, resonance)

items.name: RLC circuit: Q and bandwidth
items.doc: Resonance of a series or a parallel RLC circuit. Both resonate at f_0 = 1 / (2π × √(L × C)). The quality factor is Q = √(L / C) / R for a series circuit (R in series with L and C) and Q = R / √(L / C) for a parallel circuit (R in parallel with L and C, for example a load); the −3 dB bandwidth is BW = f_0 / Q. In the formula the exponent s is +1 for the series and −1 for the parallel circuit. Enter three of the six values; the calculator solves the rest when they determine it (f_0, Q and BW alone do not, because BW = f_0 / Q). Example with the defaults (series circuit): R = 10 Ω, L = 100 µH and C = 1 nF give f_0 ≈ 503 kHz, Q ≈ 31.6 and BW ≈ 15.9 kHz (= R / (2π × L)). For the parallel circuit enter the parallel resistance, for example 10 kΩ, which gives the same Q and BW. A Q below 1 means that the bandwidth is larger than f_0.
items.source: Series and parallel RLC resonance: f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)); series Q = √(L/C)/R, parallel Q = R/√(L/C), BW = f_0/Q; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 14 (series and parallel resonance); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

checks.warn: Q is below 1: the bandwidth is larger than the resonant frequency, the circuit is hardly selective. (For a parallel circuit R is the resistance across the tank.)

items.name: Sallen-Key low-pass (unity gain)
items.doc: Second-order active low-pass in the Sallen-Key topology with unity gain (the op-amp is a voltage follower) and two equal resistors R. C_1 is the capacitor from the junction of the two resistors to the output (feedback), C_2 goes from the non-inverting input to ground. f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × √(C_1 × C_2)) and Q = ½ × √(C_1 / C_2). C_1 = 2 × C_2 gives Q = 0.707 (Butterworth, maximally flat); C_1b shows that C_1 for the present C_2. Enter any three independent values. Example with the defaults: R = 10 kΩ, C_1 = 22 nF and C_2 = 10 nF give f_0 ≈ 1.07 kHz and Q ≈ 0.742. The op-amp is assumed ideal; its bandwidth must be much higher than f_0 and the source impedance low.
items.source: Unity-gain Sallen-Key low-pass with equal resistors: f_0 = 1/(2πR√(C_1C_2)), Q = ½√(C_1/C_2), C_1 the feedback capacitor; R. P. Sallen, E. L. Key: A Practical Method of Designing RC Active Filters, IRE Transactions on Circuit Theory, 1955; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Twin-T notch filter
items.doc: Passive twin-T notch (band-stop) filter: two T networks in parallel between input and output, one of two resistors R with a capacitor 2C to ground, the other of two capacitors C with a resistor R/2 to ground. The transfer function has a zero at f_0 = 1 / (2π × R × C), so the output is (ideally) zero there; R/2 and 2C are the shunt parts. Example with the defaults: R = 31.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF give f_0 ≈ 50.4 Hz, a notch for 50 Hz mains hum (shunt parts 15.8 kΩ and 200 nF). The notch is only deep when the parts match closely (use 1 % resistors and matched capacitors). The passive filter has a low Q (a wide notch) and needs a source impedance much lower than R and a load impedance much higher than R.
items.source: Passive twin-T network (arms R-R-2C and C-C-R/2): transmission zero at f_0 = 1/(2πRC), obtained by nodal analysis; filter textbooks, e.g. P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 6 (filters)

items.name: Pi attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive pi attenuator (π pad): one series resistor R_s between two equal shunt resistors R_p. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_p = Z_0 × (K + 1) / (K − 1) and R_s = Z_0 × (K² − 1) / (2K). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 71.2 Ω and R_p ≈ 96.2 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive pi attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_p = Z_0(K+1)/(K−1), R_s = Z_0(K²−1)/(2K); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_p must be larger than Z_0 for a pi attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: T attenuator
items.doc: Matched resistive T attenuator (T pad): two equal series resistors R_s with one shunt resistor R_p to ground between them. Terminated with Z_0 it presents Z_0 at the other port and attenuates by A dB. With the voltage ratio K = 10^(A / 20): R_s = Z_0 × (K − 1) / (K + 1) and R_p = 2 × Z_0 × K / (K² − 1). Enter any two of Z_0, A, R_s and R_p. Example with the defaults: 10 dB in a 50 Ω system need R_s ≈ 26.0 Ω and R_p ≈ 35.1 Ω. The power rating of the resistors must cover the dissipated power; this calculator does not size it.
items.source: Matched resistive T attenuator (image-impedance design): K = 10^(A/20), R_s = Z_0(K−1)/(K+1), R_p = 2Z_0K/(K²−1); Reference Data for Engineers, 9th ed. (Newnes), chapter on attenuators; formulas checked by two-port analysis

checks.warn: The attenuation must be greater than 0 dB.
R_s must be smaller than Z_0 for a T attenuator; these values do not fit together.

items.name: Inverting amplifier
items.doc: The inverting op-amp amplifier: the input signal V_in reaches the inverting input through R_in, and the feedback resistor R_f returns part of the output to the same node. With an ideal op-amp this node is a virtual ground, so the gain is A_v = −R_f / R_in and V_out = A_v × V_in. The input resistance of the stage is R_in. Example with the defaults: R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ give a gain of −10 (20 dB), so 0.1 V in gives −1 V out. The noise gain 1 + R_f / R_in = 11 sets the usable bandwidth (gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain). The output cannot exceed the supply rails.
items.source: Inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp (virtual ground): A_v = −R_f / R_in; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: An inverting amplifier has a negative gain (−R_f / R_in): a positive gain is not possible with this circuit.

items.name: Non-inverting amplifier
items.doc: The non-inverting op-amp amplifier: the signal drives the non-inverting input, and the divider R_f / R_g in the feedback path sets the gain G = 1 + R_f / R_g, which is always 1 or more (V_out = G × V_in, same sign as the input). The input resistance is that of the op-amp input and very high. Example with the defaults: R_f = 10 kΩ and R_g = 1 kΩ give a gain of 11 (20.8 dB), so 0.1 V in gives 1.1 V out. For a gain of exactly 1 leave out R_g and replace R_f by a wire (voltage follower).
items.source: Non-inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp: G = 1 + R_f / R_g; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: The gain must be above 1: a non-inverting amplifier cannot attenuate. For a gain of exactly 1 use a voltage follower (no R_g, R_f replaced by a wire).

items.name: Difference amplifier
items.doc: The classic op-amp difference amplifier with four resistors, R_3 = R_1 and R_4 = R_2: the signal V_1 reaches the inverting input through R_1, the signal V_2 reaches the non-inverting input through R_3 (which forms a divider with R_4 to ground), and R_2 is the feedback resistor. The output is V_out = (R_2 / R_1) × (V_2 − V_1): only the difference is amplified and a common-mode voltage is rejected, but only as well as the resistor ratios R_2 / R_1 and R_4 / R_3 match. The differential input resistance is 2 × R_1. Example with the defaults: R_1 = 10 kΩ and R_2 = 100 kΩ give a gain of 10, so V_2 − V_1 = 0.2 V gives 2 V out.
items.source: Difference amplifier with R_3 = R_1 and R_4 = R_2 (ideal op-amp): V_out = (R_2 / R_1) × (V_2 − V_1); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (operational amplifiers)

items.name: Summing amplifier
items.doc: The inverting summing amplifier with equal input resistors R: every input V_k reaches the summing node through its own resistor R, the currents add, and the output is V_out = −(R_f / R) × (V_1 + V_2 + … + V_n). Every input has the same gain −R_f / R, and the inputs do not influence each other because the summing node is a virtual ground. With R_f = R / n the output is the inverted average of the n inputs. Enter the input voltages as a list, for example 1 V, 0.5 V, 0.25 V. Example with the defaults: inputs of 1 V, 0.5 V and 0.25 V with R = R_f = 10 kΩ give −1.75 V.
items.source: Inverting summing amplifier with an ideal op-amp: V_out = −R_f × Σ(V_k / R); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

derived.label: G_k
derived.name: Gain magnitude per input R_f / R

items.name: Integrator
items.doc: The ideal inverting integrator: a constant input V_in through R charges the feedback capacitor C with the current V_in / R, so the output ramps linearly, V_out = −V_in × t / (R × C), starting from zero at t = 0. For sine signals the gain falls as 1 / (2π f R C) and is 1 at the unity-gain frequency f = 1 / (2π R C). A real circuit needs a resistor in parallel with C or a reset switch, otherwise offset voltage and bias current drive the output into the supply rails. Example with the defaults: 1 V into R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF (R × C = 1 ms) gives −2 V after 2 ms.
items.source: Ideal inverting integrator: V_out = −(1 / RC) ∫ V_in dt; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4

checks.warn: |V_out| is above 15 V: a real op-amp saturates at its supply rails long before this time.

items.name: Schmitt trigger
items.doc: Inverting Schmitt trigger with a reference: the input signal drives the inverting input, the non-inverting input sits between the reference V_ref (through R_1) and the output (through R_2, positive feedback). The output is at V_OH or V_OL, its saturation levels close to the supply rails (read them from the datasheet or measure them). The threshold at the non-inverting input is V_TH = V_ref + (V_OH − V_ref) × k with the output high and V_TL = V_ref + (V_OL − V_ref) × k with the output low, where k = R_1 / (R_1 + R_2). The output switches low when the input rises above V_TH and high when it falls below V_TL; the hysteresis is V_TH − V_TL = k × (V_OH − V_OL). For a design enter the four voltages and R_1 (or R_2) to get the other resistor and V_ref. Example with the defaults: a 5 V supply (V_OH = 5 V, V_OL = 0 V), V_ref = 2.5 V, R_1 = 10 kΩ and R_2 = 100 kΩ give V_TH ≈ 2.73 V, V_TL ≈ 2.27 V and a hysteresis of about 0.45 V.
items.source: Inverting Schmitt trigger with positive feedback through R_2 and a reference at R_1: V_TH, V_TL = V_ref + (V_O − V_ref) × R_1 / (R_1 + R_2); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 4; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (bistable circuits)

checks.warn: V_OH must be above V_OL.

items.name: Instrumentation amplifier
items.doc: The classic instrumentation amplifier in the three-op-amp topology: two input buffer stages share one gain resistor R_G between their inverting inputs, and a unity-gain difference amplifier (four equal resistors) forms the output stage. The differential gain is G = 1 + 2R / R_G, where R is each of the two feedback resistors of the input stage (integrated types state the sum: G = 1 + 50 kΩ / R_G for the Texas Instruments INA128, G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / R_G for the Analog Devices AD620). Only the differential input V_diff = V+ − V− is amplified by G; a common-mode voltage passes the input stage with a gain of 1 and is rejected by the output stage. Without R_G the gain is 1. Example with the defaults: R = 25 kΩ and R_G = 500 Ω give G = 101 (40.1 dB), so 10 mV differential input gives 1.01 V.
items.source: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, G = 1 + 2R / R_G (ideal op-amps, equal output-stage resistors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (instrumentation amplifiers); gain equations of the INA128 (Texas Instruments) and AD620 (Analog Devices) data sheets

derived.label: 2R
derived.name: Sum of the two feedback resistors 2R

checks.warn: The gain must be above 1: without R_G (open) the gain is exactly 1.

items.name: Capacitive reactance
items.doc: A capacitor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C). It falls as the frequency or the capacitance rises: a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies. The current through an ideal capacitor leads the voltage by 90°. Example: 100 nF at 1 kHz has X_C ≈ 1.59 kΩ. ESR, ESL and dielectric losses are ignored.
items.source: Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC) with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Inductive reactance
items.doc: An inductor opposes an alternating current with the reactance X_L = 2π × f × L. It rises with the frequency or the inductance: an inductor passes DC and blocks high frequencies. The current through an ideal inductor lags the voltage by 90°. Example: 10 mH at 1 kHz has X_L ≈ 62.8 Ω. Winding resistance and self-capacitance are ignored.
items.source: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL with ω = 2πf; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors)

items.name: Series impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in series with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The reactances are X_L = 2π × f × L and X_C = 1 / (2π × f × C); the net reactance is X = X_L − X_C, the magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²) and the phase φ = arctan(X / R) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. At resonance X = 0 and |Z| = R. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF at 1 kHz give X ≈ −96.3 Ω, |Z| ≈ 138.8 Ω and φ ≈ −43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of series RC, RL and RLC circuits (Z = R + jX, X = ωL − 1/(ωC)); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Parallel impedance (RC, RL, RLC)
items.doc: The impedance of a resistor R in parallel with an inductor L, a capacitor C or both, at the frequency f. The admittance is Y = 1/R + j × B with the susceptance B = 2π × f × C − 1 / (2π × f × L); the magnitude is |Z| = 1 / √((1/R)² + B²) and the phase φ = arctan(R × (1 / (2π × f × L) − 2π × f × C)) (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). ECalc has no unit for a susceptance, so it shows the equivalent parallel reactance X_p = −1 / B instead; at resonance B = 0, the LC branch is an open circuit and X_p is infinite (shown as –). Choose the circuit first; the component that is not used is dimmed. Example: 100 Ω, 10 mH and 1 µF in parallel at 1 kHz give |Z| ≈ 72.0 Ω and φ ≈ +43.9°.
items.source: Impedance of parallel RC, RL and RLC circuits (admittance Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)), Z = 1/Y); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 9 (sinusoids and phasors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1
formula: z = 1 / sqrt(1 / r^2 + (uc * 2 * pi * f * c - ul / (2 * pi * f * l))^2)
phi = atan(r * (ul / (2 * pi * f * l) - uc * 2 * pi * f * c))

items.name: RC time constant
items.doc: A capacitor C charges or discharges through a resistor R with the time constant τ = R × C. In general V_C = V_f + (V_i − V_f) × e^(−t/τ) with the initial voltage V_i and the final voltage V_f. Charging towards the supply voltage V_0 means V_i = 0 and V_f = V_0, so V_C = V_0 × (1 − e^(−t/τ)); discharging from the initial voltage V_0 means V_i = V_0 and V_f = 0, so V_C = V_0 × e^(−t/τ). After 1 τ the capacitor has covered 63.2 % of the way, after 5 τ 99.3 %. Example: 10 kΩ and 100 µF have τ = 1 s; charging from a 5 V supply, V_C is 3.16 V after 1 s. The chart shows V_C from 0 to 5 τ.
items.source: First-order RC step response V_C(t) = V_f + (V_i − V_f)·e^(−t/RC); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (RC circuits); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 7 (first-order circuits)

checks.warn: V_C is at or beyond the final voltage V_f (V_0 when charging, 0 V when discharging). The capacitor only approaches V_f, so no finite time reaches it.
V_C lies on the far side of the initial voltage V_i: the capacitor starts at V_i and moves towards V_f, so this value would need a negative time.

items.name: Series and parallel capacitors
items.doc: Capacitors in parallel add up: C_P = C_1 + C_2 + …. Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel: 1/C_S = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest capacitor. In series the voltage divides in inverse proportion to the capacitance; polarised capacitors in series need balancing resistors. Enter the values as a list, for example 4.7µ, 10µ, 22µ.
items.source: Series and parallel capacitor combination; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Series and parallel inductors
items.doc: Inductors in series add up: L_S = L_1 + L_2 + …. Inductors in parallel combine like resistors in parallel: 1/L_P = 1/L_1 + 1/L_2 + …, so the total is smaller than the smallest inductor. This holds only while the coils do not couple magnetically; mutual inductance is ignored. Enter the values as a list, for example 1m, 2.2m, 4.7m.
items.source: Series and parallel inductor combination (no mutual coupling); C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Capacitor energy and charge
items.doc: The energy stored in a capacitor is E = ½ × C × U² and its charge is Q = C × U; also E = ½ × Q × U = Q² / (2 × C). Any two of the four values determine the other two. Example: 1000 µF at 12 V stores 72 mJ and 12 mC. Large or high-voltage capacitors can keep a dangerous charge long after switch-off: discharge them through a suitable resistor before touching them.
items.source: Energy stored in a capacitor E = ½CU² and charge Q = CU; C. K. Alexander, M. N. O. Sadiku: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits, ch. 6 (capacitors and inductors); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1

items.name: Air-core coil (Wheeler)
items.doc: Inductance of a single-layer, close-wound air-core coil (solenoid) by Wheeler's formula: L [µH] = N² × r² / (9 × r + 10 × ℓ), with the mean coil radius r and the winding length ℓ both in inches. In the SI units used here this is L = N² × D² / (50800 × (9 × D + 20 × ℓ)) with the mean diameter D (to the centre of the wire) and the length ℓ in metres. It is accurate to about 1 % for ℓ ≥ 0.8 × r (a coil at least 0.4 diameters long) and becomes rough for shorter coils; it assumes an air core and a wire much thinner than the coil. The wire length is the helix at the mean diameter without leads. Example: 25 turns on a 20 mm diameter, 30 mm long winding give about 6.3 µH.
items.source: H. A. Wheeler: Simple Inductance Formulas for Radio Coils, Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 16, no. 10, October 1928 (single-layer coil L = N²r²/(9r + 10ℓ) in inches and microhenries, accurate to about 1 % for ℓ > 0.8r)

checks.warn: The coil is shorter than 0.4 × its diameter: Wheeler's formula is only a rough estimate here (it is accurate to about 1 % from a length of 0.8 × the radius).

items.name: Toroid inductance (A_L)
items.doc: The inductance of a winding on a ferrite or powdered-iron core follows from the inductance factor A_L of the core: L = A_L × N². Data sheets print A_L in nH per turn² (1 nH/N² corresponds to 1 mH per 1000 turns); enter it with the unit prefix, for example 250n for 250 nH. N counts the turns through the centre of the core. A_L holds for small signals below saturation and is stated with a tolerance, so the result is only as exact as the core. N_w is the turn count rounded up to whole turns. Example: A_L = 250 nH and 20 turns give 100 µH.
items.source: Definition of the inductance factor A_L of a magnetic core, L = A_L·N² (A_L in nH/N² as printed in the data sheets of ferrite and powdered-iron core makers)

items.name: Wire resistance
items.doc: DC resistance of a straight conductor: R = ρ(T) × ℓ / A with ρ(T) = ρ20 × (1 + α × (T − 20 °C)). ρ20 and the temperature coefficient α are those of the selected material at 20 °C: annealed copper per IEC 60028 (ρ20 = 0.017241 Ω·mm²/m, α = 0.00393 1/K); aluminium per IEC 60889, hard-drawn aluminium wire (ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m, the 61 % IACS value, α = 0.00403 1/K); silver is a typical handbook value. Values of real wires vary with purity and alloy. The cross-section can be entered in mm², AWG (ASTM B258) or kcmil. For a two-wire run use twice the one-way length. The linear temperature model is reliable only in a moderate range around 20 °C. Example: 10 m of 1.5 mm² copper at 20 °C have 0.115 Ω.
items.source: R = ρ·ℓ/A with ρ(T) = ρ20·(1 + α·(T − 20 °C)); annealed copper ρ20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (rounded to 0.017241) and α20 = 0.00393 1/K per IEC 60028; aluminium ρ20 = 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (the 61 % IACS value) and α = 0.00403 1/K per IEC 60889 (hard-drawn aluminium wire for overhead line conductors); silver 1.59 nΩ·m with α ≈ 0.0038 1/K as typical handbook values (e.g. CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics); AWG per ASTM B258

checks.warn: The temperature is far from 20 °C (below −50 °C or above 150 °C): the linear temperature model loses accuracy there.

formula: r = rho20 * (1 + tcr * dt) * len / a

items.name: LM317 output voltage
items.doc: The adjustable regulator LM317 holds its reference voltage V_ref (about 1.25 V) between the OUT and ADJ pins. R_1 from OUT to ADJ and R_2 from ADJ to ground set the output voltage: V_out = V_ref × (1 + R_2 / R_1) + I_adj × R_2. The adjustment-pin current I_adj (typically 50 µA) also flows through R_2. About 240 Ω is the usual value for R_1. V_ref and I_adj are typical datasheet values and vary from part to part (V_ref from 1.2 V to 1.3 V). The defaults R_1 = 240 Ω and R_2 = 720 Ω give 5.036 V. The input voltage must stay above V_out by at least the dropout voltage of the regulator.
items.source: LM317 datasheets (Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics): V_OUT = V_REF × (1 + R2 / R1) + I_ADJ × R2 with the typical V_REF = 1.25 V and I_ADJ = 50 µA

checks.warn: V_out is below the reference voltage: the LM317 cannot regulate lower than about 1.25 V.

formula: vout = vref * (1 + r2 / r1) + iadj * r2

items.name: LM317 constant-current source
items.doc: The LM317 as a constant-current source: the regulator keeps V_ref (about 1.25 V) across the resistor R between its OUT and ADJ pins, so R carries V_ref / R. The load sits between the ADJ pin and ground and also receives the adjustment-pin current I_adj (typically 50 µA): I = V_ref / R + I_adj. The resistor dissipates V_ref² / R. The default R = 10 Ω gives 125 mA with about 156 mW in the resistor. The input voltage must exceed the load voltage plus V_ref plus the dropout voltage of the regulator.
items.source: LM317 datasheets (Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics): constant-current connection with the resistor between OUT and ADJ, I = V_REF / R + I_ADJ (V_REF = 1.25 V and I_ADJ = 50 µA typical)

checks.warn: The load current is above the rated output current of the LM317 (1.5 A).
The load current must be larger than the adjustment-pin current I_adj; no resistor can set it.

items.name: Linear regulator power loss
items.doc: A linear regulator turns the voltage difference between input and output into heat: P = (V_in − V_out) × I_out + V_in × I_q, where I_q is the quiescent current the regulator draws from the input in addition to the load current. The efficiency is η = V_out × I_out / (V_in × (I_out + I_q)). The defaults (12 V to 5 V at 500 mA with 5 mA quiescent current) dissipate 3.56 W at an efficiency of 41 %; this heat has to be removed with a heat sink, or the input voltage has to be lowered.
items.source: Power balance of a series (linear) regulator: P = (V_in − V_out) × I_out + V_in × I_q; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a linear regulator needs an input voltage above the output voltage (plus its dropout voltage).

items.name: Buck converter (step-down)
items.doc: An ideal step-down (buck) converter in continuous conduction: the duty cycle is D = V_out / V_in and the peak-to-peak inductor ripple current is ΔI_L = V_out × (V_in − V_out) / (V_in × f_sw × L). The inductor current swings between I_out − ΔI_L / 2 and I_out + ΔI_L / 2, so the inductor and the switch must handle the peak current I_pk = I_out + ΔI_L / 2. Assumptions: lossless components, constant input and output voltages, continuous conduction (the valley current stays above zero); I_out is the average output current. A ripple of 20 % to 40 % of I_out is a common design target. The defaults (12 V to 5 V, 1 A, 100 kHz, 100 µH) give D = 41.7 %, ΔI_L = 0.29 A and I_pk = 1.15 A. V_out and I_out are always inputs (V_out cannot be solved from the ripple current, because two output voltages give the same ripple).
items.source: Ideal continuous-conduction buck converter (D = V_out / V_in, ΔI_L = (V_in − V_out) × D / (f_sw × L)); R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not below V_in: a buck converter can only step down.
The ripple current exceeds twice the output current: the inductor current falls to zero and the converter leaves continuous conduction, so these formulas no longer apply.

items.name: Boost converter (step-up)
items.doc: An ideal step-up (boost) converter in continuous conduction: the duty cycle is D = 1 − V_in / V_out, the average inductor current (equal to the input current) is I_L = I_out × V_out / V_in, and the peak-to-peak ripple current is ΔI_L = V_in × (V_out − V_in) / (V_out × f_sw × L). The inductor and the switch must handle the peak current I_pk = I_L + ΔI_L / 2. Assumptions: lossless components, constant input and output voltages, continuous conduction (the valley current stays above zero); I_out is the average output current. The defaults (5 V to 12 V, 0.5 A, 100 kHz, 100 µH) give D = 58.3 %, I_L = 1.2 A, ΔI_L = 0.29 A and I_pk = 1.35 A. V_in and I_out are always inputs (V_in cannot be solved from the ripple current, because two input voltages give the same ripple).
items.source: Ideal continuous-conduction boost converter (D = 1 − V_in / V_out, I_L = I_out / (1 − D), ΔI_L = V_in × D / (f_sw × L)); R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

checks.warn: V_out is not above V_in: a boost converter can only step up.
The ripple current exceeds twice the average inductor current: the inductor current falls to zero and the converter leaves continuous conduction, so these formulas no longer apply.

items.name: Smoothing capacitor
items.doc: The capacitor behind a rectifier supplies the load between the charging peaks. The peak-to-peak ripple is approximately ΔV = I / (m × f × C), where f is the mains frequency and m the number of charging peaks per mains cycle: 1 for a half-wave rectifier, 2 for a full-wave (bridge) rectifier. The estimate takes the whole period between the peaks as the discharge time and neglects the short charging time, so the real ripple is slightly lower. The defaults (1 A, 50 Hz, 1 V ripple, full wave) need 10 mF (10 000 µF). The drawing shows the bridge; for half-wave use a single diode.
items.source: Capacitor-input filter ripple estimate ΔV = I / (m × f × C) with m = 1 (half-wave) or 2 (full-wave), charging time neglected; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 9

items.name: Battery runtime
items.doc: The runtime of a battery follows from its capacity and the load current: t = Q × usable fraction / I. The usable fraction is the part of the rated capacity you can actually draw; the cut-off voltage, ageing, low temperature and high discharge currents reduce it. The defaults (a 2500 mAh cell, 250 mA load, 80 % usable) run for 8 hours. The calculation assumes a constant load current; the rated capacity is only valid for the discharge rate stated in the cell's datasheet.
items.source: Definition of charge Q = I × t (1 Ah = 3600 C, SI Brochure, BIPM) with a usable-capacity fraction; background: D. Linden, T. B. Reddy (eds.): Handbook of Batteries, 3rd ed. (capacity depends on discharge rate and temperature)

checks.warn: A usable fraction above 100 % is not possible: more energy is drawn than the battery holds.

items.name: Battery charge time
items.doc: The charge time follows from the capacity and the charge current: t = Q / (I × η). The charge efficiency η is the share of the supplied charge that ends up stored; the rest is lost. With a constant-current/constant-voltage charger the current also tapers off near the end, which lengthens the real time further. The default of 80 % is a planning assumption, not a datasheet value; use the charge figure of the battery's datasheet where there is one. The defaults (2500 mAh, 1 A, 80 %) give 3.125 h (3 h 7.5 min).
items.source: Definition of charge Q = I × t (1 Ah = 3600 C, SI Brochure, BIPM) with a charge efficiency; background: D. Linden, T. B. Reddy (eds.): Handbook of Batteries, 3rd ed. (charging of secondary cells)

checks.warn: A charge efficiency above 100 % is not possible: more charge would be stored than supplied.

items.name: Battery pack (series/parallel)
items.doc: A pack of N_s cells in series and N_p such strings in parallel: the pack voltage is N_s × the cell voltage, the pack capacity is N_p × the cell capacity, and the stored energy is the product of both. The defaults (3S2P with 3.7 V, 2500 mAh cells) give 11.1 V, 5 Ah and 55.5 Wh. The cell voltage is the nominal voltage: a fully charged lithium-ion cell is higher (about 4.2 V), an empty one lower. Real packs also need cell balancing and protection.
items.source: Series connection adds voltages, parallel connection adds capacities, E = U × Q (1 Wh = 3600 J); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 and 9

checks.warn: The number of cells in series must be a whole number.
The number of strings in parallel must be a whole number.

items.name: Cable voltage drop
items.doc: Voltage drop of a copper or aluminium cable: ΔU = b × ρ × L × I × cos φ / A with the resistivity ρ at the conductor temperature, the one-way cable length L and the conductor cross-section A. b is 2 for direct current and single-phase AC (outgoing and return conductor) and √3 for three-phase AC (drop between the lines); cos φ does not apply to DC. The percentage is related to the nominal voltage U_n. Resistivity at 20 °C: copper 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028), aluminium 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60889); it rises with the temperature coefficient 0.00393 /K for copper (IEC 60028) and 0.00403 /K for aluminium (IEC 60889). The cable reactance is neglected, which is acceptable for small cross-sections; it adds to the drop at large cross-sections. The defaults (copper, single-phase 230 V, 20 m, 16 A, 2.5 mm², cos φ = 1, 70 °C) give about 5.3 V (2.3 %). Safety: mains voltage is dangerous. The results are guide values only; the design of a mains installation must follow the installation standard (for example DIN VDE 0100-520 or IEC 60364-5-52) and the local rules, and must be done and checked by a qualified electrician.
items.source: Resistive voltage drop of a conductor ΔU = b × ρ × L × I × cos φ / A; cf. IEC 60364-5-52 and DIN VDE 0100-520 (voltage drop in consumers' installations); resistivity at 20 °C of annealed copper 1/58 Ω·mm²/m with α = 0.00393 /K (IEC 60028) and of hard-drawn aluminium 0.028264 Ω·mm²/m with α = 0.00403 /K (IEC 60889)

checks.warn: The voltage drop is above 5 %: check the permissible value in the installation standard, and use a larger cross-section or a shorter run.
cos φ cannot be larger than 1.

formula: du = b * rho_t * l * i * cosphi / a

items.name: LED series resistor
items.doc: An LED needs a series resistor that takes up the part of the supply voltage the LEDs do not use: R = (V_S − n × V_F) / I_F for a string of n LEDs in series. Parallel strings each get their own resistor, so the supply delivers m × I_F in total; never let several parallel strings share one resistor. Example with the defaults: a 12 V supply and two strings of three red LEDs (V_F ≈ 2 V) at 20 mA need 300 Ω per string; the supply delivers 40 mA (0.48 W), and half of that power is lost in the resistors. Take V_F from the datasheet for the chosen current; it varies with colour, current and temperature.
items.source: Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law for an LED string (the LED as a diode with a forward voltage); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (LEDs and diode circuits)

derived.label: η
derived.name: Share of the power in the LEDs

checks.warn: The supply voltage does not exceed the forward voltage of the string: no resistor can set the current.
The number of LEDs per string and the number of strings must be whole numbers.
The resistor dissipates more than 0.25 W: use a resistor with a higher power rating.

items.name: Zener regulator
items.doc: A shunt regulator: a series resistor R feeds a Zener diode in parallel with the load. R must pass the maximum load current I_L plus the minimum Zener current I_Z(min) that keeps the Zener in regulation: R = (V_in − V_Z) / (I_L + I_Z(min)). Without load the whole current flows through the Zener, so its power is V_Z × I_R at no load, the worst case. The Zener is treated as ideal (dynamic resistance neglected). Use the lowest input voltage to size R and check the powers with the highest. Example with the defaults: 12 V to 5.1 V at 20 mA load and 5 mA minimum Zener current needs 276 Ω (270 Ω is the nearest E24 value); the Zener then dissipates about 0.13 W without load.
items.source: Zener shunt regulator (series resistor R = (V_in − V_Z) / (I_L + I_Z) with an ideal Zener); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (Zener diode regulators)

checks.warn: V_in must be above V_Z: otherwise no current flows through the series resistor.
The resistor cannot supply the load current plus the minimum Zener current (one of the currents comes out negative).
The Zener dissipates more than 0.5 W without load: a 500 mW Zener is not enough.
The series resistor dissipates more than 0.25 W: use a resistor with a higher power rating.

items.name: Transistor switch
items.doc: An NPN transistor as a saturated low-side switch: the base resistor must pass enough base current to drive the collector current I_C into saturation. The minimum base current is I_C / h_FE; the overdrive factor multiplies it (a factor of 2 to 10 is common) so that the transistor stays saturated despite spread and temperature: I_B = overdrive × I_C / h_FE and R_B = (V_in − V_BE) / I_B. Use the minimum h_FE from the datasheet at this collector current, not the typical value. Example with the defaults: a 5 V logic output switching 100 mA with h_FE = 100 and an overdrive of 5 needs 5 mA of base current and R_B = 860 Ω. The forced gain h_FE / overdrive is the ratio I_C / I_B the circuit actually uses.
items.source: Saturated BJT switch (R_B = (V_in − V_BE) / I_B with I_B = overdrive × I_C / h_FE); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2

checks.warn: V_in does not exceed V_BE: no base current can flow.
Overdrive below 1: the base current is smaller than I_C / h_FE, so the transistor does not saturate.

items.name: BJT divider bias
items.doc: DC operating point of a common-emitter stage with voltage-divider bias (four resistors). The divider R1 / R2 is replaced by its Thevenin equivalent, V_TH = V_CC × R2 / (R1 + R2) with R_TH = R1 ∥ R2, and the base current is taken into account: I_B = (V_TH − V_BE) / (R_TH + (β + 1) × R_E), I_C = β × I_B, I_E = (β + 1) × I_B, V_E = I_E × R_E, V_B = V_E + V_BE and V_CE = V_CC − I_C × R_C − I_E × R_E. The model assumes the forward-active region; this calculator is forward-only (enter all seven values). Example with the defaults: 12 V, R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, R_C = 4.7 kΩ and β = 100 give I_C ≈ 1.29 mA and V_CE ≈ 4.66 V. The warning for a soft divider appears when R_TH exceeds a tenth of (β + 1) × R_E: then I_C depends noticeably on β.
items.source: Voltage-divider bias with the Thevenin base circuit and (β + 1) × R_E; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 2; A. S. Sedra, K. C. Smith: Microelectronic Circuits (BJT biasing)

checks.warn: V_TH does not exceed V_BE: the transistor is off and the model does not apply.
V_CE is below 0.2 V, a typical saturation voltage: the transistor is saturated and the active-region result is not valid.
The base divider is soft: R_TH is more than a tenth of (β + 1) × R_E, so I_C depends noticeably on β.

items.name: MOSFET losses
items.doc: Estimated losses of a MOSFET that switches the current I_D against the voltage V_DS at the frequency f_sw with the duty cycle D. Conduction loss: P_cond = D × I_D² × R_DS(on). Switching loss with linear, overlapping voltage and current transitions: P_sw = ½ × V_DS × I_D × (t_r + t_f) × f_sw. Gate-drive loss, output-capacitance loss, reverse-recovery and body-diode loss are not included, and R_DS(on) rises with temperature, so enter the value at operating temperature from the datasheet. The calculator is forward-only. Example with the defaults: 10 A at 12 V, R_DS(on) = 10 mΩ, D = 50 %, t_r = t_f = 20 ns and 200 kHz give 0.5 W conduction plus 0.48 W switching, 0.98 W in total.
items.source: Conduction loss D·I²·R_DS(on) and the linear-transition switching loss ½·V·I·(t_r + t_f)·f_sw; R. W. Erickson, D. Maksimović: Fundamentals of Power Electronics (switching loss); N. Mohan, T. M. Undeland, W. P. Robbins: Power Electronics (power MOSFET losses)

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.
The switching times take more than half of the period: the linear switching-loss model does not apply.

items.name: Heatsink
items.doc: Steady-state thermal model of a power device: a chain of thermal resistances from the junction to the ambient air, T_J = T_A + P × (R_thJC + R_thCS + R_thSA), with junction-to-case, case-to-heatsink (insulator, grease) and heatsink-to-ambient resistance. Every stage drops P × R degrees. Enter the maximum junction temperature of the datasheet as T_J (for example 125 °C or 150 °C) together with the power and the other resistances to find the heatsink resistance R_thSA you need; a result of zero or below means no heatsink is good enough. Example with the defaults: 10 W at 25 °C ambient with 1.5 + 0.5 + 3 °C/W gives a junction temperature of 75 °C.
items.source: Steady-state thermal resistance network (the thermal analogue of Ohm's law: ΔT = P × R_th); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed. (heat and power design)

checks.warn: The junction temperature is above 150 °C, a common absolute maximum for silicon power devices: check the datasheet limit.

items.name: NE555 astable (oscillator)
items.doc: Astable multivibrator with an NE555 timer: the capacitor charges through R_1 + R_2 up to 2/3 of the supply and discharges through R_2 down to 1/3. The high time is t_H = ln 2 × (R_1 + R_2) × C (ln 2 ≈ 0.693), the low time t_L = ln 2 × R_2 × C, the frequency f = 1 / (t_H + t_L) = 1.44 / ((R_1 + 2 R_2) × C) and the duty cycle D = t_H / (t_H + t_L) = (R_1 + R_2) / (R_1 + 2 R_2), which is always above 50 %. Enter any three independent values (for example f, D and C to design the resistors). Example with the defaults: R_1 = 1 kΩ, R_2 = 68 kΩ and C = 10 nF give about 1.05 kHz at 50.4 % duty cycle (t_H ≈ 478 µs, t_L ≈ 471 µs). With the control pin not driven the result does not depend on the supply voltage; real parts add the tolerances of R and C, leakage and switching delays, so very high frequencies and very small resistors deviate.
items.source: NE555 datasheet (Texas Instruments NE555 / SE555 precision timer), astable operation: f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)·C), t_H = ln 2·(R_A + R_B)·C, t_L = ln 2·R_B·C; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (timers)

checks.warn: The duty cycle is not above 50 %: a standard NE555 astable cannot do that (R_1 would be zero or negative). A diode across R_2 allows lower duty cycles.

items.name: NE555 monostable (one-shot)
items.doc: Monostable (one-shot) with an NE555 timer: a trigger pulse at pin 2 starts the output pulse, during which the capacitor charges through R from 0 up to 2/3 of the supply. The pulse width is t = R × C × ln 3 ≈ 1.0986 × R × C (the datasheet rounds this to 1.1 × R × C). Enter any two of R, C and t. Example with the defaults: 100 kΩ and 10 µF give a pulse of about 1.1 s. The trigger pulse must be shorter than the output pulse; the real width varies with the capacitor tolerance and leakage (use film or low-leakage capacitors for long times).
items.source: NE555 datasheet (Texas Instruments NE555 / SE555 precision timer), monostable operation: t_w = 1.1·R_A·C, exactly ln 3·R_A·C (charging from 0 to 2/3 V_CC); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (timers)

items.name: Crystal load capacitors
items.doc: Load capacitors for a parallel-resonant quartz crystal in a Pierce oscillator: two capacitors C_1 = C_2 from the crystal pins to ground. The crystal sees the load capacitance C_L = C_1 × C_2 / (C_1 + C_2) + C_stray, where C_stray is the pin, trace and board capacitance (a few pF as a rough estimate, 2 to 5 pF). With C_1 = C_2 = C this gives C = 2 × (C_L − C_stray). Take C_L from the crystal datasheet. Example with the defaults: C_L = 18 pF and C_stray = 4 pF give C_1 = C_2 = 28 pF (use the nearest standard value, 27 pF).
items.source: Load capacitance of a parallel-resonant crystal in a Pierce oscillator: C_L = C_1·C_2/(C_1 + C_2) + C_stray (series connection of the two capacitors plus stray capacitance); the crystal datasheet states C_L; P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 7 (crystal oscillators)

checks.warn: C_stray is not below C_L: the board already provides the load capacitance, no load capacitors are needed (or the crystal needs a lower load capacitance).

items.name: Frequency, period and duty cycle
items.doc: Converts between the frequency f, the period T = 1 / f and the duty cycle D of a rectangular signal: t_high = D × T and t_low = T − t_high. Enter any two independent values (the frequency and the period alone do not fix the duty cycle). Example with the defaults: 1 kHz at a duty cycle of 30 % is a period of 1 ms with 300 µs high and 700 µs low.
items.source: Definitions: frequency f = 1/T (hertz = 1/s, SI Brochure, BIPM) and duty cycle D = t_high/T of a periodic rectangular signal

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.

items.name: PWM average voltage
items.doc: Average and RMS value of a rectangular PWM signal that switches between V_low and V_high with the duty cycle D: V_avg = V_low + D × (V_high − V_low) (a low-pass filter, or the inertia of a motor, LED or heater, turns the PWM into this DC voltage) and V_rms = √(D × V_high² + (1 − D) × V_low²) (the heating effect in a resistive load). Enter any three of D, V_high, V_low and V_avg. Example with the defaults: 25 % duty cycle between 0 V and 5 V gives V_avg = 1.25 V and V_rms = 2.5 V.
items.source: Average and RMS value of a rectangular two-level waveform over one period (integration of the waveform); P. Horowitz, W. Hill: The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., ch. 1 (signals)

checks.warn: The duty cycle must be between 0 % and 100 %.

items.name: PCB trace width (IPC-2221)
items.doc: Current-carrying capacity of a printed-circuit trace after the IPC-2221 equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725, with the current I in A, the temperature rise ΔT in °C and the copper cross-section A in mil² (1 mil = 25.4 µm). The constant k is 0.048 for traces on external layers and 0.024 for internal layers. The cross-section is the copper thickness times the trace width; 1 oz copper is a layer of about 35 µm. The defaults (2 A, 10 °C rise, 1 oz, external) need a trace about 0.78 mm (31 mil) wide. The IPC-2221 curves cover temperature rises of about 10 °C to 100 °C and currents up to about 35 A. The result is a guide value for a single trace: neighbouring copper, vias and the board thickness change the real temperature rise, and the newer IPC-2152 gives more detailed data for critical designs.
items.source: IPC-2221 (generic standard on printed board design), current-carrying capacity equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 with k = 0.048 (external) and k = 0.024 (internal layers); see also IPC-2152

checks.warn: The current is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 35 A); the result is an extrapolation.
The temperature rise is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 100 °C); the result is an extrapolation.

items.name: PCB trace resistance
items.doc: Resistance of a copper trace: R = ρ × L / (W × T), with the resistivity at the trace temperature ρ = ρ_20 × (1 + α × (θ − 20 °C)). For copper ρ_20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (17.24 nΩ·m) and α = 0.00393 /K (annealed copper, IEC 60028). The voltage drop is R × I and the dissipated power R × I². The sheet resistance R_sq = ρ / T is the resistance of a square of any size. The defaults (0.25 mm wide, 35 µm thick, 50 mm long, 25 °C, 1 A) give about 0.1 Ω, so 0.1 V and 0.1 W. Enter the temperature of the trace, not of the room: at the temperature rise of a heavily loaded trace the resistance is noticeably higher.
items.source: Resistance of a prismatic conductor R = ρ × L / A; annealed copper ρ_20 = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m and α = 0.00393 /K per IEC 60028; resistivity at temperature ρ = ρ_20 × (1 + α × (θ − 20 °C))

items.name: Via current capacity
items.doc: Estimate for a plated through-hole via. The copper barrel is a tube of length H (the board thickness) with the finished hole diameter D and the plating thickness T_p, so its copper cross-section is A = π × T_p × (D + T_p) and its resistance at 20 °C is R = ρ × H / A with ρ = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028). The IPC-2221 equation is written for traces; applying it to a via barrel is a common engineering approximation, not a rule of the standard. Here the barrel cross-section is used with the constant for internal layers: I = 0.024 × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 (A in mil²), which is the lower of the two IPC-2221 constants. Several vias in parallel share the current. The defaults (0.3 mm finished hole, 25 µm plating, 1.6 mm board, 10 °C rise) give A = 0.0255 mm², R = 1.08 mΩ and I = 0.95 A.
items.source: Tube cross-section A = π × T_p × (D + T_p) and R = ρ × H / A with ρ = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028); current from the IPC-2221 equation I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 with the internal-layer constant k = 0.024 applied to the barrel as an approximation

derived.label: I
derived.name: Current for the temperature rise (IPC-2221, internal)

checks.warn: The temperature rise is above the range of the IPC-2221 curves (about 100 °C); the result is an extrapolation.

items.name: AWG wire size conversion
items.doc: American Wire Gauge: the diameter of the gauge n is d = 0.005 in × 92^((36 − n) / 39) (ASTM B258), a factor of about 1.123 per gauge step and about 2 for every 6 steps. The cross-section is A = π / 4 × d². Enter the diameter in AWG, mm, mil or inch, or the cross-section in AWG, mm², kcmil or mil²; a circular mil is the area of a circle 1 mil in diameter, so 1 kcmil = 0.5067 mm². The gauges 0000, 000 and 00 are −3, −2 and −1. The default AWG 10 is 2.588 mm in diameter and 5.261 mm² (ASTM B258 lists 2.588 mm). The resistance of 1 km is for annealed copper at 20 °C (1/58 Ω·mm²/m).
items.source: ASTM B258 (standard nominal diameters and cross-sectional areas of AWG sizes of solid round wires): d = 0.005 in × 92^((36 − n) / 39); 1 circular mil = π / 4 mil²; copper resistivity 1/58 Ω·mm²/m (IEC 60028)
